opus-5.5.text:
Simulation is really central to everything we do. The way I see it, for learning-based robotics, and especially reinforcement learning for legged robots, the simulator is essentially where the robot gets its experience. You can't realistically have a physical quadruped fall over millions of times while it figures out how to walk, but in simulation you can, and you can do it massively in parallel.

That was a big part of the motivation behind our work on GPU-based simulation. Instead of running one or a handful of robots on a CPU, we run thousands of robots simultaneously on a single GPU. That turned training times that used to take days or weeks into something like minutes. When you can train a locomotion policy in twenty minutes, it changes how you do research. You can iterate on reward design, try different terrains, tweak the curriculum, and get feedback almost immediately.

Building the environment itself is a big part of the work, and it's not just the physics engine. You have to think carefully about the terrain you generate, how you structure a curriculum so the robot starts on easy ground and gradually moves to stairs, slopes, and rough terrain, and how you randomize things like friction, mass, motor strength, and sensor noise. That randomization is really what lets the policy survive the jump to the real robot, because no simulator is perfect. You're not trying to make the simulation match reality exactly. You're trying to make reality look like just one more variation the policy has already seen.

So I see the simulator less as a perfect digital twin and more as a training ground. Its job is to be fast, diverse, and close enough to reality on the things that matter. The sim-to-real gap is still there, and a lot of engineering goes into the actuator models and the observation design to close it. But once you get that pipeline right, you can deploy policies on hardware zero-shot, and that's been really exciting to see.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. For me, simulation is really the heart of the whole approach. When I started working on legged locomotion at ETH, the bottleneck in reinforcement learning for robots wasn't the algorithms, it was the data. You just can't collect enough experience on a physical robot. It's slow, it's expensive, and the robot breaks. So the question became: how do we generate experience at a scale where learning actually works?

That's what led to the massively parallel simulation work, running thousands of robots at once on a single GPU with Isaac Gym. Suddenly a policy that would have taken weeks to train could be trained in minutes. And that changes how you work. You stop treating each training run as precious and start iterating on the reward design, the curriculum, the randomization, almost like a conversation with the environment.

But I'd say the environment itself is where most of the real engineering happens. People sometimes think of the simulator as a given, and the learning as the interesting part. In practice it's the opposite. Deciding what terrain to generate, how to randomize the physics parameters, what noise to inject into the observations, how to model actuator dynamics, all of that is what determines whether the policy transfers to the real robot. The sim-to-real gap is closed mostly by being thoughtful about the environment, not by clever algorithms.

So I see building simulation environments as the core design tool. It's the place where you encode what you want the robot to be robust to, and it's the interface between what's possible in the real world and what the learning system can actually discover.

r002.rationale: The response says the bottleneck was data, not algorithms, and does not state that Rudin’s team develops custom reinforcement-learning algorithms to use the environments more fully.

astra-6.text:
I see simulation as a tool that lets us iterate much faster. With reinforcement learning, the robot needs to try a lot of things, and many of those attempts will fail. In simulation, we can run many robots in parallel and let them explore without damaging hardware.

But the goal isn’t necessarily to build a perfectly realistic world. It’s to capture the things that matter for the behavior we want to learn: the dynamics of the robot, its contact with the ground, and the observations and actions available to the policy. We can also vary those conditions during training so the policy doesn’t depend on one exact model.

Then testing on the real robot closes the loop. You find out which assumptions were reasonable and which differences actually affect performance, and that tells you where to improve the simulation.

sol-6.1.text:
I see simulation as a tool for developing and testing the learning system. With reinforcement learning, the robot needs to interact with its environment many, many times, and doing all of that on hardware would be slow and difficult. In simulation, we can run many robots in parallel and let them explore, fall over, and try again.

The important question is what the simulator needs to capture for the behavior you want to learn. You need the relevant dynamics and contacts, but you also have to account for the fact that simulation will never perfectly match the real robot. So you train across variations in the environment and the robot’s properties, rather than letting the policy depend on one very specific setup.

Ultimately, the goal isn’t just to get something that works in simulation. It’s to build a training environment that produces behavior that also works on the physical robot.
